The Aṃśumat Tantra.
The Ritual of Consecration with a Conch Shell (Śaṅkhābhiṣecanavidhi).
I shall explain the consecration with a conch shell; let it be heard with focused attention. It bestows long life, prosperity, and victory over death, and destroys disease.
...and the liberation from desires... increasing sons and grandsons.
It is declared to be pacifying and nourishing, destroying all evils.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the consecration with the water of the Śaṅkhatoyā river...
on the Rohiṇī nakṣatra when conjoined with Saturn, and likewise on the Puṣya nakṣatra when conjoined with Jupiter.

When conjoined with the hand of the Sun (the Hasta nakṣatra), when joined with Bhṛguvār (Friday), when joined with Mars (*), and also when Mercury is in Anurādhā, and when conjoined with the Moon and Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa)—provided it is favorable to the sacrificer. (*) Note: The text fragment "kuje... suggests the conjunction with Mars (Bhauma-vāra/Tuesday). The ellipsis indicates a missing portion of the verse. (†) Note: The text fragment "budhānurādhakepi ca" indicates the conjunction of Mercury with the nakṣatra Anurādhā. (‡) Note: The text fragment "somavaiṣṇava saṃyukte" indicates the conjunction of the Moon with the nakṣatra Śravaṇa (Vaiṣṇava). The asterisked portions are reconstructed based on the context of astrological conjunctions.
On the eighth day, on the new moon day, at the transit [of the sun],
and on whatever birth-star of the sacrificer it may be, one should perform the consecration with conch water.
It is said that the conch is of three kinds: male, female, and neuter.
That which is thick at the base is female; however, that which is thick at the tip is neuter.
If the tip and the base are equal, it is proclaimed to be masculine;
the conch should be known as fourfold, according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
...one should bestow the true nature of the bow, established equally in the mind.
Having filled the belly, it is here called the Brahma-conch.
Likewise, the conch of a Kṣatriya is yellowish-white;
that of a Vaiśya is remembered as being long at the base and light.
The conch of a Śūdra is light, long, and short-backed;
thus has the characteristic of the conch been described, and hence this city is called Śaṅkhottara.
The conch originating from Tāmraparṇī is proclaimed as the best;
that from the Gaṅgā is middling, and that from the Narmadā is inferior.
Thus, the threefold [classification] has been stated; now the origin of the conch is described here. A conch that spirals to the right is traditionally known as the best of its kind.
Having placed that conch in the center, one should arrange other conchs around it;
and with the characteristics previously described, one should fill it with [water] by means of such-and-such [a person].
Half of that is the middle [size], and half of that again becomes the lowest. A conch shell with a clockwise spiral is prescribed according to its own measurement.
It is shown to be exceedingly beautiful when placed before the object of worship, adorned with emeralds and other gems.
Having established one with a thousand conchs, it is proclaimed as "excellent" (uttama);
one with a hundred conchs is, in due order, the "middling" (madhyama);
and one with forty-nine conchs is proclaimed as the "inferior" (kanyasa).
Thus, one should worship in due order according to the rules as prescribed for the ritual bathing;
or else, by way of assistance, one should consecrate [the image] with water from a conch shell.
Having worshipped Vighneśvara, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should then employ the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual bathing and carry out the procedure as previously prescribed.
He should arrange the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) in separate vessels.
Then, having taken a water vessel, he should fill it with water;
it should be joined with that very substance [the aforementioned powder] and with fragrant flowers and the like.
Having wrapped the mouth [of the vessel] with a cloth, the wise man should place it there.
For the purpose of the ritual procedure for the worship of the conch, one should place a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front [of it].
Having worshipped Vighneśvara, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Then the wise man should wash the conch with *tuṣā*...
The triangle with Śaṅkha at its feet is indeed [thus]...

The characteristic of the line... and Sarasvatī is at the tip of the conch.

And the conch, [beginning] from Īśvara and ending at the head, and the seven notes... [the third]. One should place the conch-shell in the middle of these other vessels that hold the stream. One should worship the three principles (*tattva*) by way of the continuous path of the channels (*nāḍī*).
Attachment, determination, knowledge, art, and time... [are the constituents of] delusion (*mohaka*).
Knowledge, the Lord (*Īśvara*), and the Nameless (*Anākhya*) are remembered as the triad of powers (*śaktitraya*).
Having mixed it with scented water, one should apply the eight fragrances.
One should place the eightfold Śaiva fragrance consisting of sandalwood, nāgakeśara, camphor, mālatī, water-lily, saffron, uśīra,
and kuṣṭha. One should also arrange the sandalwood with the mantra "gandhadvārām".
One should place agarwood with the Śivagāyatrī mantra;
one should place camphor with the "śanno devī" mantra;
and one should place tamāla with the "kitavāsa" mantra.
One should place water and saffron with the *tatvāyāme* mantra;
one should place uśīra and saffron with the *nākesuparṇya* mantra;
and one should place [the substances] and the *ra...* chamber with the *trimūrtameti* mantra.
Having performed churning with the *kūrca* [mantra], or else with the mantra "yad vā devāya," one should meditate upon the Bhāgīrathī in the center, possessing half a body and four limbs,
with palms joined in reverence and adorned with all ornaments.

Having invoked Gaṅgā— who is clothed in waves and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts— one should meditate upon her and offer incense and lamps. At the conclusion of the worship with the conch, one should worship the water vessel.
Having prepared a firm base with rice, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Having placed a three-legged stand in the center, one should set down a vessel upon its half-height.
Having wrapped it all around with a cloth, one should fill it with scented water.
Having invoked the ninety sacred sites (navatīrtha), one should offer fragrant substances along with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped thoroughly with incense and lamps, one should then perform the worship of the door; having set aside that substance, one should then cause an oil massage to be performed.
One should apply a paste of wood-apple (*āmalaka*), wood (*kāṣṭha*), and turmeric (*rajanī*);
then, having set out the bath-water, one should also [anoint it] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the nectars (*amṛta*).
At the conclusion of the consecration with fragrant water, one should meditate upon the mantra-flower;
having offered milk-rice as the food offering, one should cause garments and perfumes to be given.
One should perform the conch-consecration with the Rudrasūkta mantra,
as well as the Camaka, the Puruṣasūkta, the Śrīsūkta, and the Pāvamāna hymns.
Having firmly placed the conch of the Ācārya four finger-breadths before the liṅga,
the wise one should cause that water to flow [over it], and then he should bathe [the deity] with other [substances].
At the conclusion of each respective number [of recitations], the discerning one should perform worship.
Bathing water, clothing, and fragrance, as well as a garland of flowers;
likewise, food offerings, betel, incense, and lamps.
One should perform the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) with exactly sixteen services;
having taken up the Śiva-pitcher upon the head of the attendant.

One should perform a circumambulation of the temple, fully equipped with all types of ornaments; then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should stand upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of Śiva.
Having taken [the water] from the pitcher into the vessel, one should place it in the center of the *liṅga*.
One should also place the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*) upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with the *vardhanī* vessel.
One should bathe the *liṅga* with the *vardhanī*, while the pitchers are for the pedestal.
One should not place [the vessel] from the jar... and indeed should arrange it... Having offered water, one should present the mantra.
Thus, by means of circumambulation according to the rule, one should perform the remainder of the twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) in another manner.
...he shall attain that meritorious state of mortals.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the conch-consecration (*śaṅkhābhiṣeka*) in the *Aṃśumantatantra*. [Section:
The Milk-Bath (*kṣirasnāna*).
Thereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the milk-bath (*kṣīrasnāna*),
which bestows the fruits of longevity and health and destroys all diseases.
For the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons, it shall bring peace to the world.
It may be of three kinds: mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*), scattered (*vikīrṇa*), and combined (*samyoga*).
Having taken up full milk, one should set it aside according to the prescribed rule;
this is called "mixed. Now hear about the "scattered" [type].
Having brought together the Śiva-aṅgāras, one should cause them to be heard [recited] over a vessel of hot water;
one should place them upon the top of the liṅga, joined with ten drops of flowing heat.
This is known as the "scattered single or double" (*ekadvikīrṇa*); now listen constantly to the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
The ritualists, having taken a tree, should fashion four-legged supports.
It is recorded that the height of these four legs above the liṅga should be ten aṅgulas.
Having drawn a lotus in their center, there should be a hollow in the middle of that [lotus].
In the center of that, the wise one should place a jar of milk containing jewels.
This is called "the conjunction," performed together with the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*). Five cows have arrived from the city of Śivā for the worship of Śiva.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Sumanā, Surabhi, and Suśīlakā; Kapilā, Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmravarṇā, Raktā, and likewise Śvetā—
these are proclaimed as the colors for Nandā, Bhadrā, and Sumanā.

For the purpose of sacrificing to the gods and for the welfare of all beings, the cows stand as mothers; they are auspicious for the sake of Subhadra and for Śiva. The gods always abide in the cows, and by means of the cows, the sacrifice proceeds.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally situated at the base of the horn;
Kumbha stands at the tip of the horn, the source of both the stationary and the moving.
The Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) is said to be on the forehead, and Hara (Śiva) is situated in the middle of the neck.
The four Kābālas are located at the navel, likewise residing in the cavities;
the Aśvin gods are in the ears, and the Moon and Sun reside in the eyes.
The Marut gods are in the teeth, and Varuṇa resides in the life-force (jīvā).
Sarasvatī is in the *huṃ* syllable, and Yama and Yakṣa are on the two cheeks. (l.
6) The Gandharvas are in the middle of the hooves, and the Pannagas are at the tips of the hooves;
likewise, the hosts of the Parās are at the rear tips of the hooves. (l. 7)
One should establish the ten Rudras in the ten channels for the sake of left-handed accomplishments.
The Pitṛs reside on the slope of her hips, while Umā would be in her chest. (v.
8) O Śrī Varānane, the piles [of the fingers] are likewise always measured in finger-breadths.
The rays of the sun, the hairs [on its body], the cow’s urine, and likewise the Gaṅgā;
all the Kuṣas and the lords of all remain situated here in this Amṛta. ... free from passion ... those. The four oceans ... and those which are in the milk of the cows.
Just as whatever vigor exists in the world, that is to be known as the essence of milk.
Therefore, one should perform the milk-bath with every effort.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the milk-bath in the *Dīpta-śāstra*.
From nine up to a thousand... Oṃ...
(p.6b, l.1) Dhātrī, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and likewise Mṛḍā; Durgā, Kāntī, Mohinī, Uṣā, and the goddess Sundarī. (l.2)
Bhuvaneśī, likewise Karṇā, whose sole form is the Great Mantra;
the Yoginī who destroys the bow [of Māra], who is all-pervading and has the nature of the Bindu;
Saṅgrāmaṇī, the power of victory, the destroyer of calamities, and whose form is victory.
Vaiṣṇavī, Bhaktapoṣā, and Brahmātmakāmarūpiṇī;
Sukhāsinī, Padmavatī, Dravyarūpī, and Caṇyagā;
Kṛpālinī, Mahāsenā, and Tārā—these are the thirty-two deities.
The retinues of all male deities consist of twenty-eight members;
likewise, the retinues of all female powers (*śakti*) consist of thirty-two.
For the sake of the purpose arising from all the Tantras, I shall perform the worship of Gaurī’s pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

Having prepared the *arghya*—consisting of auspicious water (*puṇyāha*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—along with red sandalwood and flowers in a copper vessel; having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*;

and having dispelled the obstacles located in the sky above and below with the *astra-mantra*, one should gaze upon it with "Homage to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*). Then, one should perform the worship of Uṣā at the southern quadrangle of the eastern gate.
Facing the east, one should perform the worship of Uṣā at the door. Having meditated [on her] with the mantra: "To Uṣā-mūrti, obeisance" in the west; (l.

10) "Oṃ hāṃ, to Daṇḍin, obeisance" in the south; "Oṃ hāṃ, to Piṅgala, obeisance" in the north; "Oṃ hāṃ, to Gaṇāmbikā, obeisance" in the southeast; (p. 7a, l. 1) "To Tārā, obeisance" in the northeast. Salutation to Ārādhyā. Salutation to Paramasukhā. Having worshipped the lotus seat in the center, [one worships] at the tips of the filaments starting from the east: salutation to Dīptā; salutation to Sūkṣmā; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Jayā; salutation to Bhadrā; salutation to Vidyā; salutation to Vimalā; salutation to Amoghā;
salutation to Adyutā. In the center, salutation to Sarvatomukhī. In the middle of the lotus seat: *oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to Uṣāsanā.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Uṣā; oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Uṣā. Obeisance to Khaṭhotkala, the consort of the form of Uṣā. Having performed the placement of the five Brahmans, the meditation [is as follows]:
[I meditate upon her] who possesses the beauty of a full-blown lotus and resembles the rising sun.
Uṣā possessed a pair of eyes like blue lotuses and was endowed with the auspicious marks on all her limbs.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the goddess Uṣā. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, having applied the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having performed the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, one should worship her with the ritual services (*upacāra*). Having displayed the lotus-mudrā and the image-mudrā, [one recites]: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the goddess Uṣā. [Then] Oṃ hāṃ, [and so on for] the heart and other limbs. Having displayed the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), [one worships] at the tips of the petals: obeisance to Soma-śakti; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Aṅgāraka-śakti; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Budha-śakti; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati-śakti.

*Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śukra-śakti. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara-śakti. (L. 2) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Rāhu-śakti. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ketu-śakti.* Having worshipped thus, having displayed the *namonta-mudrā*, having honored [the deities] with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), having recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) as much as possible, having offered the fruit of the recitation to the Goddess, and having presented the supreme mouth-offering (*paramamukhārghya*), one should worship *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Tejacaṇḍeśvarī* in the northeast and then perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). Thus one should perform the worship of Uṣā.
Having gone out from the southern gate, washed his feet, sipped water (*ācamana*), and re-entered, he stands facing north.

Having performed the application of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*), the ritual of making oneself one with the deity (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), he sprinkles [the area] at the door with "Oṃ hāṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ. [He then offers:
"Homage to the eastern *śānti*-archway (*toraṇa*); homage to its passion (*rāga*); Oṃ, homage to Śvetā; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kṛtayugā; homage to Bhūlokā."

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhuvarloka. (l. 9) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Āditya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma. On the tridents: Oṃ, obeisance to Pūṣan. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhātṛ. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidhātṛ. Homage to Suvarlokā. Homage to Mahallokā. (p. 8a, l. 1) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka. Homage to Budha. On the tridents: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhārgava. Homage to Parjanya. Homage to Aśokā. (l. 2) Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, [one worships] along the western gateway:
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bālatoraṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vajra. (l. 3) Homage to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dvāparayuga.

Salutation to Satyaloka. Oṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara. Salutation to Rāhu. Salutation to Ketu. Upon the tridents: Oṃ, salutation to Aryaman; salutation to Mitra; salutation to Satya; salutation to Dhanada; salutation to Śrīpradā. Having performed the offering of water for the feet and the other rites.
To the south of the eastern gate, having worshipped the root-form of Durgā on the first jar—
she who is of a reddish-yellow and glossy complexion, wearing a crown of sandalwood and jewels,
wrathful, with red eyes, fierce, and white fangs.
I worship Durgā, the power of Bhaga, whose form is battle, who bears hands mangled in combat and a face contorted with rage, and who grants boons while roaring like a thundercloud.

Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃśa... Having worshipped the petals and so forth, [the practitioner] who possesses the great mantra, having first worshipped the seat and the form with the root mantra at the eastern side of the southern gate in a separate water-jar,
[visualizes] the radiance [and] the limbs, tender with enchantment.
On full moon days, she assumes various guises.

I remember with my mind the Great... (l. 4) the Tamed One, O Great Manuja. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to the Great Mantra of the Vidyā-kalā; [having worshipped] the seat-form... (l. 5). Having performed the worship, one should worship the root-mantra of the Āpaghnī seat-form on the first jar to the south of the western door.
I take refuge in the supreme one, who resembles the brilliance of fire, who is the abode of bliss,
who has not yet reached the lotus-abode, and who is the friend of Āpava.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā Āpaghnī. Having invoked and fully worshipped her, one should worship the seat-form and the root-mantra of the one of divine form in a separate water-pot to the west of the northern door:
"She who is renowned as resembling the sun, adorned with divine gold..."
I worship Śivā, who holds a staff in her hand, has long eyes, and possesses a divine form.

Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the door of the *kala* of installation for the one of divine form (*divyarūpī*). Having invoked and fully worshipped [her], one should again, at the second jar on the right of the eastern door, worship the seat, the image, and the root-mantra of the goddess Kāntī.

I worship the Goddess Kānti— the Mistress of the Universe, the Protectress of the World, who bestows happiness upon those who bow to her— she who is dyed with madder, adorned with a garland of Bhr̥ṅgarāja flowers, whose teeth are revealed, who is clothed in blue garments like a rampart, whose two deep wings obstruct the quarters of space, who possesses a universal form, and who has two horns.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kāntidevī. Having worshipped her with water for the feet and other offerings, one should again worship the seat of Mṛḍānī in the first jar to the north of the eastern gate:
"She who has a red luster, wears red garments, has the sun and moon as her eyes, and is adorned with jewel ornaments..."
Wearing silver armlets and necklaces, possessing great and superior virtues, she dwells upon the summit of the peak of Mount Meru.
I worship Mṛḍānī, whose limbs are enchanting, who grants boons to those who bow before her, and who is skilled in all [tasks].
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mṛḍā. Having performed the ritual services (*upacāra*) at the western jar of the southern door, one should worship the single-formed seat, the image, and the root-mantra.
I worship the Great Goddess Jayātmikā, the Mistress of Victory, who resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon a throne with latticed feet.

Oṃ hāṃ (hrāṃ) hrīṃ, obeisance to Jayarūpiṇī. Having worshipped [her] at the second pitcher to the south of the western door, and having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra of Jayaśakti—
[her who is] eternal, five-faced, and resembling jasmine flowers.
One should always remember her, who has the form of victory and is served by the wielder of the discus.
Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jayaśakti. Having worshipped her, [one should worship] the Puṇyagāsana-mūrti at the eastern jar of the northern door. (l.
9) [One should worship her who is] the presiding deity over the three cities (*puratraya*), seated upon a lotus throne.
I worship the Great Queen Pātragavatī, the meritorious Nāyikā... [l.
10] ...homage to her. Having offered [this], again, to the west of the northern gate, at the second pitcher: Padmāvatī...
having worshipped the root-form on the seat of Īśvara, the meditation is as follows—
With white radiance and golden earrings,
with two arms adorned by hanging lotuses,
and with a face graced by beautiful earrings upon his two eyes.
And then, situated upon a fragment in the eastern direction.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Amṛteśvara*. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), bringing near (*sannidhāna*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*) with the Sadyojāta mantra, and having displayed the six-faced mudrā; having offered the water for honor (*arghya*) with the mantra ending in *svāhā*; having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamps; and having placed a handful of *darbha* grass upon the *pālikā* vessel: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vaikartana; obeisance to Vivasvat*.

Salutation to Mārtāṇḍa. Salutation to Bhāskara. Salutation to Ravi. (l. 6) Salutation to the Illuminator of the World. Salutation to the Witness of the World. Salutation to Trivikrama. Salutation to Āditya. Salutation to Śivasūrya. (l.
