"Let us know the one with the horse-banner; let us meditate upon the one with the lotus in hand; may that Sūrya inspire us. Having thus invoked [the deity], having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to all the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, having presented milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and having offered incense and a lamp, one should prepare milk in a vessel of gold or other material and worship it with: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Amṛtaśakti."
The seeds of sesame, mustard, mung bean, black gram, rice, *priyaṅgu*,
horse-tail grass (*śvadaṃṣṭrā*), barley, and *asvakanda*— these are the seven grains (*saptadhānya*). Having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥsaṃskāra*),
having worshipped them with the *Saṃhitā*, and having empowered them with the mantra "the seed of Śiva" (*śivabīja*), one should mutter the *Oṣadhīsūkta*.

Having recited the mantra beginning with *namo hiraṇyabāhave* and ending with *namassahamānāya*, one should deposit [the seeds] into the *pālikā* vessels and other containers. Having worshipped them with "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," one should worship [them] with "Obeisance to Vaikartana and the others. This is the sowing of the seeds (*bījāvāpa*). One should pour milk-water twice with the mantra and once silently, together with a conch, auspicious items, and a bull.

Having nourished [the seed] with water from a moon-pitcher, one should again fill it with pitcher-water every day. One should fill it with earth after offering incense and lamps. At the conclusion of the rite, one should release the pitcher and its stand at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). Thus ends the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*).

Now, the procedure for the tying of the auspicious thread (*kautukabandhana*) is described. On the night preceding the day appointed by the astrologer, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) with rice on the day of the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*). Having drawn a lotus in its center and strewn sesame seeds, parched grain, and *darbha* grass upon it, one should place the mechanical device (*yantrikā*) in its middle. Then, having filled a small bowl (*sthalikā*) placed over that with rice—

Having placed a coconut, gold, silver, cotton thread, and ashes; having purified that thread with water and smeared it with white sandalwood paste; and having placed the thread upon the coconut on top of rice—for the sake of the festival of Maheśa:
[this is for] Maheśa... Balinātha, Astrarāja, Vighnarāja, the staff of Skanda’s banner, the bull, the sacrificial pedestal, and the forms of the devotees.

Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) twice with "rakṣo... and so forth, and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited, [one should worship] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*... on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*): "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. (l. 10) On the base of the *yantrikā*:
"Obeisance to Tryambaka. On the pedestal (*sthalikā*): "Obeisance to Prakṛtitattva. On the rice grains (*taṇḍula*): "...obeisance.

"Obeisance to the seventy million great mantras (*saptakoṭimahāmantra*). (l. 11) On the gold and silver threads: "Obeisance to Ananta. Having worshipped [the deity] on the linen and cotton threads... [one should proceed].
Regarding the application of the ashes: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Agni, the lord of splendor, who holds a spear in his hand, whose vehicle is a ram, and who is accompanied by his retinue.

Having offered [the oblation] beginning with the feet, one says: "Salutation to this seat in my own vessel. [One should visualize him as] dark-hued, holding a mace in his hand, and seated upon a buffalo.
[Having invoked] those with sprout-like hands, adorned with all ornaments—
[saying] "Obeisance to Yama, the Lord of the Pretas, who holds a staff in his hand, whose vehicle is a buffalo, who is accompanied by his retinue, and who is clothed"—
and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other honors, [one should say] at the pitcher of Nirṛti: "Obeisance to the seat of Nirṛti."
Niṛṛti is dark-complexioned, equipped with a sword and a shield;
he is formidable, of demonic form, the enemy of hungry ghosts, and has mantras for his eyes.
"KṢAṂ! Homage to the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who holds a sword in his hand, whose vehicle is a vetāla, who possesses a thousand [attendants], together with his retinue.
Having thus invoked him and offered incense and lamps, one should say: "Homage to the seat of Varuṇa in the Varuṇa-vessel.
[I invoke] Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, who is black in color and possesses great strength."
With the moon on another hand, granting boons, and adorned with all ornaments.

"Salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of waters, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a makara, and who is accompanied by his retinue. Having thus worshipped and offered incense and lamps, [one should worship] in the wind-pitcher:
"Salutation to Vāyu, the abode of the wind."
Anila is smoke-colored and is accompanied by a deer as his mount;
he carries a goad in his right hand and a snake in his left.

Or [one should offer] to Vāyu, the lord of breath, who holds a banner in his hand, whose mount is a deer, together with his retinue and weapons: "Homage! Homage to him together with his retinue! Having offered the water for the feet and so forth, up to the incense, [one should place it] in the lunar jar (*somakumbha*) with the words: "Homage to the seat of Kubera."
[He is] the lord of the yakṣas and others, with a mace in hand, white in color, seated upon a horse, two-armed, with a red face, possessing lotus-like eyes, and holding a lotus in his hand. (l.
2) Saṃ, to Soma, the lord of the protectors, who holds a mace in his hand, who has a horse as his vehicle, together with his [retinue]. (l. 3)

"Salutation to Sahasrāra together with his retinue. Having thus worshipped, and having offered the items from the foot-water (pādya) up to the lamp, [one worships] in the Īśāna-pitcher: "Salutation to Īśāna. (l.
4) "Īśāna has four arms, three eyes, and wears matted hair."

Having worshipped with the mantra: "Obeisance to Īśāna, the Lord of Knowledge, who holds a trident in his hand, is mounted upon a bull, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; together with his retinue and weapons," and having fully honored him with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with the lamp.
In the eastern jar of Nirṛtikumbha: "Obeisance to Viṣṇuvāsana,

who has a dark-complexioned body as his vehicle, wears yellow garments, possesses two eyes, and has four arms, [holding] the conch, the discus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons."

"Salutation to Anantādhi-Viṣṇu, the lord of the earth, who holds a discus in his hand, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya, together with his retinue and weapons. Having thus worshipped and offered [substances] from the foot-water (pādya) up to the lamp, [one should place them] in the southern jar of the Īśāna-jar: "Salutation to the seat of Brahmā (brahmāsana)."
Brahmā, four-faced, the Sustainer, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣamālā*),
mounted upon a swan— having invoked him together with [the other deities] endowed with four arms.
To the Lord of the World, the water-pot, the two doors, the earth, the elements, and the hand-bearer...
One should take sixteen squares for the feet and nine squares for the center... one should provide a central nave of nine squares together with twenty-seven squares.
This is the procedure for the nine *kuṇḍas* and the five-shrine pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Likewise, there is one jar for the deceased and one jar for the dog.
Having warded off the six [deities]—Śiva, Varuṇa, and the others—from the southern nave and the southwest, one should ward them off from the north as well.
The Kumbha [deity] should be in the northeast; Triyakumbha in the north;
and Īśa, Brahmā, Mahākāla, Śānti, Nandi, and Tribhāskara in the east.
Agni, Yama, Vighneśa, Vidyā, Bhṛṅgin, and Śavāstupā;
Viṣṇu, Nirṛti, Ramā, Skanda, Nivṛtti, and Astrapāśin;
Vāyu, Vighna, Caṇḍakalā, Devī, Soma, and Guru, in due order.

One should install the teachers: those born from the pair of glorious banners, who delight in the art of the gateway of the sun; those who protect the site of women; those whose bodies consist of the earth and its parts; those who possess ten actions and knowledge; and those who protect the assembly of circles.
For Indra, [the mudrās] are slightly reddish, black, smoky-colored, moon-bright, gold-colored,
lotus-shaped, and like crystal;
and for the Creator (Vidhātṛ) starting from the east, they are red, O Lord of Brahmā.
Blue in the southwest, and multicolored in the center;

having fashioned the eight banners in this manner, one should install them at the arches, gates, and thresholds. [One should worship] Praśānta, Śaśidhara, Dīpaṭṭā, Loka-vikrama, Vāstu, Lakṣmī, Gaṇapati, Guru, Yama, and the other Vidyeśvara jars.

Having placed these auspicious [vessels]— along with the *kumbha* and *vardhanī*, characterized by the proper marks, accompanied by their ritual manuals (*āvidhāna*), provided with cords and mechanical fittings, their bases adorned with mango leaves, gold, jewels, and various grains— each in its appropriate position; and having brought together from all sides the makers of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements, who have performed their ablutions...

Having performed the *mahālaya* rite together with his two perpetual fire-maintainers (*nityāgnika*), his teachers, and his assistants, and having performed the worship of the Sun (*sūryapūjā*), he should first worship the deities beginning with Saura in the jar situated between the two *indrapāvakas*.
Immediately thereafter, having gone outside, washed his feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should again enter within, facing north.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, and having prepared the general arghya-water together with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should recite the mantra *astrāya hūṃ phaṭ* ten times. Beginning from the eastern gate, one should worship in due order.
One should join the arches (*toraṇa*) to the arches and worship the lords of the gates at the pitchers (*kalaśa*). One should worship in sequence as before.

Salutation to Śāntitoraṇa. ... Salutation to Śvetā. Salutation to Kṛtayuga. On the tridents: salutation to Pūṣan; salutation to Sāvitrī; salutation to Vidhātrī. (l. 10) Salutation to Bhūloka; salutation to Bhuvarloka; salutation to Soma; salutation to Aṅgāraka; salutation to Pratyuṣas; salutation to Prabhāsana. (l. 11) Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] at the southern gate-arch: salutation to Bhūtitoraṇa; salutation to Yajurveda; salutation to Tretāyuga. (l. 12)

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Bhārgava on the spikes; salutation to Parjanya; salutation to Indra; salutation to Aśoka; salutation to Suvarloka; salutation to Maharloka; salutation to Budha; salutation to Bṛhaspati; salutation to Ajaghanyā," [he should worship] at the western door-arch with "Salutation to the strength-arch.
Having recited [the remaining mantras], and having had various kinds of wild animals collected by an attendant, he should enter the city immediately.

Having entered the city quickly before the day of mounting the chariot—at the conclusion of the evening protection rites prior to the day of mounting the chariot—the preceptor should perform the offering of the *tīrtha* and the *aṅkura* according to the previously stated procedure. Having performed the remainder as before, from the worship of the pavilion for the eight directional guardians up to the offering of the *bali*, [he should offer] to the *rakṣasa* deity of the directional *bali* with the mantra "namaḥ. The *bali* substance is... rice (*odana*).

Having offered the *bali* from [the east] to the northeast—consisting of clarified butter, goat meat as a substitute, non-putrid red flowers, and [reciting] "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā; svāhā to the Rākṣasa"—and having adorned the Great Lord (*Maheśa*) for his departure to Mount Kailāsa, having given silver as a gift for the sake of the journey, and having caused the procession to proceed, the deities of the procession enter the pavilion of the assembly. [Recite]: "Svāhā to the deities of the hunting expedition! (l. 8).

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items, having presented fruits, [meat from] hunting, and so forth, and having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the sake of the procession.

Having performed the worship of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa-pūjā*) and so on, up to the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali-dāna*), at the time of dawn, one should perform the mounting of the chariot (*rathārohaṇa*) at the conclusion of the daily worship (*nitya-pūjā*). Then, having honored the chariot with oil and having adorned it, and then having adorned Maheśa and placed him upon the chariot or similar vehicle, [one proceeds].

Rising together with the *śaktis* amidst the sounding of the five musical instruments (*pañcavādya*) and preceded by various other instrumental strains, [he] mounts the chariot... (p. 13a, l. 1) ...having adorned [it] with [garments]. Having offered coconuts, plantains, pieces of sugarcane, portions of mung beans, jackfruit, betel leaves, and so forth, (l. 2) ...and having presented the food offerings (*naivedya*). Having offered camphor and thus performed the circumambulation, he enters the special pavilion (*maṇṭapa*). (l. 3) Having given the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*).

Having offered cakes made of flour and cakes made of black gram (*māṣāpūpa*), and having performed the incense offering, the lamp offering, and the sixteen ancillary services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should give betel-leaf and water to the devoted people and install [the deity] in the primary location. One should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) according to the procedure prescribed for the bathing ceremony. Then, the festival of the seventh day is concluded.
Thereafter, at the morning festival, having adorned Kaṅkālanātha prior to the festival, one should offer flowers, garments, sandalwood paste, and ornaments upon the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Having adorned [the deity], having smeared him with ashes, and having taken up a full alms-bowl; having caused Devadāsī to be smeared with ashes, one should pray to Tākṣa...

properly. One should cause the procession to be made, performing a circumambulation of the village. Having entered the temple and offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamps, and having presented them, the festival of the alms-round (*bhikṣāṭana*) is concluded. Immediately thereafter, having adorned Subrahmaṇya on a horse-carriage, one should cause the hunting expedition (*mṛgayātrā*) to be conducted.

For that purpose, having adorned Maheśa and entered the forest together with those wearing various costumes, he, being stationed there, [recites]: *Oṃ skandāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ bījāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ aṅkurāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ nālāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ mukulāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ kaṇḍakebhyo namaḥ* | *Oṃ kesarabhyo namaḥ* | *Oṃ karṇikāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ hāṃ mahāpadmāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Vāmā and ending with Manonmanī; having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva (śivāsana)"; "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (śivamūrti)";
and "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva"; and having invoked [the deity]; having offered a welcome and the arghya water with the right hand, and having offered incense and a lamp;
[he offers] rice mixed with ghee, mung-bean rice, jaggery rice, curd, milk, guṇālā cakes, and black-gram cakes.
Having offered sweetmeats accompanied by vegetables, one should present them with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.

Having performed the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) for the lamp of Śiva, one should again offer prayers with serpent-garlands for the sake of increasing all ornaments. Thus ends the procedure for hoisting the banner (*dhvajārohaṇavidhi*) according to the *Kāmika*.
Now, the procedure for the festival of the meal offering (bhaktotsava) is described.
In the evening, at the conclusion of the *saukhya* [ceremony], having adorned the reciter of hymns with the *bimba*, *vasu*, *sūtra*, and other ornaments,
and having likewise adorned Jisāviśvara upon a palanquin; the ascetic, taking up his staff, upper garment (*uttarīya*),
and water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) along with the people in due order, was presented with an alms-bowl filled with rice grains and provided with bound food.
Having swept the streets with brooms and taken up [the vessels], one should cleanse the thoroughfares.

Having swept the street and filled [the vessels] such as the *pālikās* and others, one should conduct the festival of the devotees accompanied by all musical instruments. Having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should place [the deity] in its own place. One should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the sake of the procession.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the festival of devotion.
Then, as before, one should perform the evening protection and worship. (l.
13) In front of the deity, in the vicinity of the banner, one should perform the invocation of the nine deities.
One should prepare three sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*): in the center, the west, and the east. (p. 14a, l. 1)
...having placed [the drum] in the west, one should set down the *bherī* drum in the east.
Likewise, in the center, the best of preceptors should cause the *puṇyāha* proclamation to be recited.
[Then follow] the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*), the worship of Vināyaka, and the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the worship of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) for the purpose of beating the drum," he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited. Having set out the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should place the King of Weapons upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and worship it. [He should offer salutations] with "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti and the others," and having worshipped the King of Weapons with its seat, form, and root-mantra.
Having thus invoked [the deities], and having performed the rites beginning with invocation and ending with the offering of incense and lamps, one should worship as follows:
on the middle petal of the King of Weapons (Astrarāja)—*oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the southern petal—*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*;
on the left petal—*oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*.
On the blade: *namaḥ* to Pārvatī. On the trident: *namaḥ* to Kumbhasenānī. At the mouth of the jar: *oṃ hāṃ namaḥ* to Vināyaka. (l.

6) At the tip of the staff: *namaḥ* to Madana. In the middle of the staff: *namaḥ* to Bhāskara. At the base of the staff: *namaḥ* to Caṇḍeśvara. On the eastern petal: *namaḥ* to Mahālakṣmī. (l. 7) On the southern petal: *namaḥ* to the Seven Mothers. On the western petal: *namaḥ* to Jyeṣṭhā.

On the northern petal, "Salutation to Kātyāyanī. Having thus worshipped the eight kings [of the directions], one should strike the drum. Having covered the drum with a new cloth: "Salutation to Nandin on the south; salutation to Mahākāla on the north; salutation to Rudra in the center.
Having worshipped [them] in this manner with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having offered a piece of coconut and betel leaf, one should present the food offering, incense, and lamps.

In the center of the drum: *namaḥ* to Mahālakṣmī. To the south and north: *namaḥ* to Brahmā; *namaḥ* to Viṣṇu. In the southern ring: *namaḥ* to Sūrya. In the northern ring: *namaḥ* to Candra. At the seven pegs: *namaḥ* to the Seven Mothers. At the nine pegs: *namaḥ* to the Nine Planets.
On the handle: *namaḥ* to Skanda. Having thus worshipped and offered the seat and other requisites, facing eastward, [he recites] *brahmajajñānam* on the right.
"Ut-uttare idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame" (Rig Veda 1.22.17)—with this, he strikes twice. "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe"—this is the third strike.

Afterwards, for the purpose of invoking the deities, he should inform Śiva: "I shall perform the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*); having performed its ancillary rite, the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapapūjā*), I shall also perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) for the sake of purification. Having made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) twice, [he prepares] the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*).

Having set out the special *arghya* offering, and then having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship the Sun, together with his limbs and retinue, in the solar water-pot situated between Indra and Agni. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[He is] resembling golden saffron, with two lotus-like hands displaying the gestures of granting boons.
He is endowed with the boon of fearlessness and adorned with all ornaments.

Having meditated thus: (l. 4) Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ; having worshipped the root-form seated upon the throne of Śiva-Sūrya; having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings; having gratified [the deity] with betel and other items; having recited the root mantra one hundred times; having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering; having stood up and gone outside; having washed his feet and hands; having sipped water; and having sprinkled the doors with ordinary arghya water using the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, at the eastern archway: *Namaḥ śāntitoraṇāya*. *Oṃ hāṃ bhadratoraṇāya namaḥ*.
At the south: *Oṃ hāṃ bhūtitoraṇāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ vijayatoraṇāya namaḥ*. At the west: *Oṃ hāṃ balatoraṇāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ vajratoraṇāya namaḥ*. At the north: *Oṃ hāṃ ārogya*...

"Oṃ, salutation to Toraṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nīlalohitāraṇa. Having thus worshipped the deities of the archways (toraṇas), having offered water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings, having honored them with incense, lamps, betel-leaf, and so forth, and having performed circumambulation once more, [one should proceed] to the northern jar at the eastern gate.
She has four faces and four arms, is black in complexion, and possesses great strength;
she holds a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, wears a snake as her sacred thread, and bestows peace.

Having reflected thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Śāntikalā [deity]. Having offered the food offering, incense, and lamp, [one should place them] in the pitcher to the south of the eastern door.
The wise one should meditate upon Nivṛtti, who has the luster of molten gold, is adorned by four faces like moons, and holds a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus.
Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the door of the Nivṛtti-kalā*. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp, [one worships] at the western jar of the northern door:
[the goddess] resembling pure crystal, four-faced and four-armed.
Holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is adorned with jewels of consecration.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp, [one proceeds] again to the southern jar at the eastern door:
[I salute] Nandin, who has three eyes, is endowed with matted locks, possesses four arms, and is renowned for his learning.
And he also holds a trident and a thread, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nandin; salutation to Gaṅgā*. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp, [one should worship] in the second pitcher to the south of Īśāna:
"The one with a garland of skulls, large-mouthed, with ears for arms and a great belly."
He had three eyes, thick black limbs, and a beard and hair that were dark brown.

Having meditated thus: "He carries a staff and a sword in his right [hands], and a shield and a trident in his left," one should offer food, incense, and a lamp to Mahākāla. [Then, one should place him] in the western jar at the southern gate.
Four-armed and three-eyed, Bhṛṅgīśa has a tawny complexion;
he holds the gesture of granting fearlessness and an axe in his right hands, and the gesture of boon-granting and a trident in his left.
Alternatively, Bhṛṅgīśa is fleshless-bodied, white, holding a staff and a rosary;
he is eternally three-eyed, wears a topknot, and is intent upon the world of Śiva.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin*. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp, [one should worship] Gajānana—three-eyed, saffron-colored, and four-armed—in the second pitcher to the west of the fire.
He carries a noose, a goad, a tusk, and a ripe mango fruit.

Having meditated thus: "The Lord of Obstacles (Vighnanāyaka) has a jeweled body and holds a trunk and a left hand," one should offer food, incense, and a lamp with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃṃ vighnarājāya namaḥ*.
Then, at each door, on the northern pitcher:
"The bull has the form of a bull, three eyes, and the luster of jasmine, the moon, and snow;
he is the support of all, the soul of the universe, with sharp horns and great strength.
Having thus meditated upon the bull together with his consort Śakti, one should offer: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull (Vṛṣabha). Then, having offered food, incense, and a lamp.
In the second vase to the north of the Rākṣasa [direction],
there is a youth with one face and a serene countenance, red in color,
possessing four arms, appearing as a child, and adorned with golden ornaments.
Holding a spear and a cock in his hands, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
he may be either seated or standing, adorned with a crown and a casket.
One should worship Guha, who is attended by Śrīvallī and Devasenā.
Having meditated thus, and having offered the food offering (naivedya), incense, and a lamp, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda;
obeisance to the Goddess," at the eastern jar of the northern door.
She has one face and two arms, is adorned with all ornaments, stands upon a lion, is yellow in color, and holds a trident and a mirror in her two hands.
She wears a crown-jewel box adorned with pearls and other gems;
or else, she is the Goddess with a gracious countenance, her hands graced by white water-lilies.
Or else, she may be adorned with a jeweled casket-diadem and pearl necklaces;
or rather, the goddess with a gracious countenance, her hands resplendent with the *kala-hāra* gesture.

One should contemplate [the deity] as having a pericarp: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Goddess Śrī*. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp, [one should worship] Caṇḍeśvara at the second pitcher to the east of Vāyu—he who has four faces, four arms, and three eyes.
It possesses a crest, a garland, and a trident, and is endowed with a casket and a crown.
He bears a water-pot, a trident, a rosary, and an axe;
he is enriched by a sacred thread of great passion, and his two ears are adorned with earrings.

Having meditated thus: "He who has the luster of a fresh cloud and who regulates the *samaya* and other [observances]," one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp to Caṇḍeśvara with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ caṇḍeśvarāya namaḥ*.
[This is done] at the northern *kalaśa* of the Rākṣasa.
Seated upon a lotus throne, yellow in color, with two eyes,
possessing a thousand pairs of lotuses, she was a maiden with eyes like lotuses.
Having meditated thus:

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Having offered the food offering, incense, and lamp, and having worshipped each with water for the feet and other offerings, one should thereafter worship the eight banners starting from the east.
Red in color, beginning with Praśāntā, they all have two arms and two eyes;
their palms are joined in reverence, and they are adorned with various ornaments.
Having thus recollected: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the banner named Praśānta in the east;
obeisance to the banner named Śiśira. In the south, obeisance to the banner named Parjanya;
obeisance to the banner named Jayanta. In the west, obeisance to the banner named Sañjīva; obeisance to the banner named Amṛta."
In the north: "Salutation to the banner named Dhanada. Having thus worshipped, one should thereafter perform the worship of the ten weapons, beginning with the Vajra.

One should place the qualities of the weapons, such as the excellent Vajra, in order starting from the east—[deities] who have one face, two eyes, and who always hold [their respective] weapons in their hands.
Having thus recollected:
in the east,
Vajra is the firm añjali, described as "thick and hard."
With a serene soul, you [should be] among these [beings] in the region of the eastern direction, which is worthy of worship by those who come before you.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vajra. In the southeast: Śakti has the form of a woman, with a red body and a triangular shape.
Their very nature will become one of provocation toward the venerable fire on the edge of the horizon.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śakti. On the right:
The staff is indeed a man, black, with copper-colored skin and red eyes.
One should worship him, whose nature is the qualities (guṇas), in the direction of Yama at the base of the Saubhava [mandala].
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Daṇḍa; in the southwest (Nairṛti). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Khaḍga.
And Khaḍga is a dark-blue man with cruel, wrathful eyes;
he is described as being of a tender nature—one should worship him in the southwest (Nairṛta).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Khaḍga. Furthermore, these [are]:
the noose, all seven hoods, the male [deity], and the male [seed-syllable] joined together.
This pervasive self is indeed pervaded; [this is] the worship of Vāruṇī performed a hundred times.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose.
In the northwest.
The yellow man Aṅkuśa, who has turned away from this [world], possesses great arms;
he is proclaimed as Vikṛtātman and is worshipped by all in the northwest. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aṅkuśa.
In the north:
Gadāpītā, a maiden with broad and fleshy hips;
she is renowned as the essence of mantra—one should worship her from the direction of Kaubera.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the mace. In the northeast:
the trident-bearer, whose body is dark blue like the sky.
This [image] should have the form of an armlet; one should worship Umā in the northeastern direction.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the trident. To the right of Īśa: Padma, Pūṣan, Divya, Śukrāṅga, and Śubhalocana.
This [is] indeed Mahāpadma, to be worshipped to the right of Īśa. (l. 7) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Padma.
In the southwest (Nairṛti).
A hundred-spoked wheel, with the syllable *hrūṃ*, shaking and rattling, dark-bodied, and male;
this lotus-natured one is to be worshipped on the side of Nirṛti, while the other [wheel] is from the east.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the discus.
Having thus worshipped the ten weapons, one should worship the eight elephants: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the elephant Airāvata; salutation to the elephant Puṇḍarīka.
Salutation to Vāmanagaja. (l. 10) Salutation to Kumudagaja.
Salutation to Añjanagaja. Salutation to Puṣpadantagaja.
Salutation to Sārvabhaumagaja. Salutation to Suprītakagaja. (l. 11)
Having thus worshipped the eight elephants, one should again resort to the western door. Having sprinkled the door with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), [one should worship]:
"Salutation to Pataṅga" on the wooden plank above it;
"Salutation to Bhuvaṅga" on the plank above that; "Salutation to Gaṇeśa" on its right side; and "Salutation to Sarasvatī" on its left side.

Having worshipped with "Homage to Nandin! Homage to Mahākāla! Homage to Yamunā!", one should gaze at the western door with the root mantra. Having cast a flower there with the *astra* mantra, one should strike both sides above it with the *astra* mantra. Having struck the bell and the palm of the hand with that same [mantra], [one should do so] with the *astra* of the intermediate heaven.

Having joined [the threads], one should expel [the obstacles] from the left side of the western door with the *astra-mantra*. Having joined the eastern, southern, and northern doors with the *astra-mantra*, and having visualized the obstacles as having emerged from the left side of the western door and settled upon one's own left hip, one should thereafter touch the body of the thread while moving clockwise around it. Having entered the interior of the pavilion—
For the sake of destroying all obstacles, one should worship the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) in the western-northern flask.

One should worship the King of Garments (*vastrarāja*), who bestows boons according to one's capacity, holding a *māyākunda* flower, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his hands.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the King of Weapons, the destroyer of all obstacles. Then, in the second pitcher to the east of the [direction of] Niṛṛti, [one should worship] Vāstunātha, who is white, peaceful, and has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (l. 9)
Holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left hand.

Having meditated thus: "He is seated there upon a svastika, established on a white lotus throne," [one should offer] *oṃ hāṃ vāstvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Having presented the food offering, incense, and lamp, (l. 11).
The Armor of the Weapon-mantra.
Having protected the sacrificial pavilion with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), [one should assign:
"Homage to the earth element" to the pillars of the pavilion;
"Homage to the water element" to the grasses. (l. 12)
In the bonds: obeisance to the fire element. In the bamboo beams: obeisance to the air element.
In the pillars: obeisance to the space element.
Having spread *darbha* grass upon the center of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and having placed the water-pot (*kumbha*),
the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: [He is] radiant like the midday sun, bearing the moon, blazing with a terrifying, loud laugh.
One should meditate upon Paśupati, the Lord who has the form of a divine weapon: three-eyed, adorned with serpents, with a moon on his crest and a beard, with shimmering hair,
the all-pervading one holding a trident, a mallet, a sword, and a spear in his lotus-like hands,
possessing fangs and four faces like snow.
Three-eyed and four-armed, fierce, and endowed with matted locks along with the Śakti,
he wears yellow garments and holds a noose, an arrow, and a trident.
Having thus meditated with the mind upon the Pāśupata weapon— which possesses the power to favor all beings and accomplishes every desired object— one should perform the sacrifice.
*Oṃ haṃ ślīṃ klīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Pāśupatāstra.* Thus one should invoke.

Having performed the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkṛti*), one should display the nine mudrās. One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the root mantra. To the south, [one should place] a fist-sized vessel for the *vardhanī* separated by a distance.
Having meditated upon the Mistress of the Weapon (*Astraiśvarī*), who is seated upon a lion-throne, positioned facing westward, red in color, with blazing hair, and holding a sword and a shield,
one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

"Oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the power of the Pāśupata weapon. Having thus invoked [the deity], performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, and worshipped [her], one should worship in the inner area of the pavilion, starting from the east and extending to the northeast (īśāna). That is as follows: at the second pitcher to the right of the eastern gate.
One should worship Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who is yellow in color, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata,
possesses a thousand eyes, and is stationed in the eastern quarter.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. (l. 6) Obeisance to the lord of the gods, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand;
obeisance to him whose vehicle is an elephant, together with his limbs and his retinue.
[This is] in the pitcher of the southeast direction.
One should meditate upon Agni mounted upon a goat, red-bodied and red-eyed,
endowed with seven flames and the Śakti, holding a rosary and a water-pot,
carrying a *sruva* and a *sruk* ladle, three-eyed, and moon-crested.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni, the lord of splendor, who holds a spear in his hand, whose vehicle is a ram, who holds a spear in his hand, together with his retinue.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) at the sites of the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) using the *prāsāda* root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the mantras for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting with the heart, and having worshipped him with the three *tattvas*, one should offer the water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) as before.

Having bathed [the deity] with the water for the *arghya* offering, following the sequence beginning with the anointing (*abhyaṅga*) and ending with the ritual bathing (*snapana*), and having offered the water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the *arghya*, one should present the perfumes and flowers and request permission for the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the *īśāna* face. Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the form of the *tatpuruṣa* face. Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the form of the *aghora* face. Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the form of the *vāmadeva* face.

Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Heart. Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the form of the Head. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the form of the Crest. Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the form of the Armor. Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the form of the Weapon. Having thus worshipped and displayed the five mudrās (or the five-faced mudrā), one should worship the second enclosure.
Salutation to Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and to the Lord Śikhaṇḍin.
This is the third enclosure. Salutation to Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Skanda, Devī, and Caṇḍeśvara.
This is the fourth enclosure. Salutation to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna.

"Salutation to Brahmā for Viṣṇu. (L. 2) This is the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). Having worshipped the fifth enclosure with the mantra: "Salutation to the thunderbolt, spear, staff, sword, noose, goad, mace, trident, lotus, and discus," (L. 3) and having offered incense and lamps, one should worship the seat and the fundamental form (*mūrti*) of Manonmanī in the *vardhanī* vessel. One should worship the seats and fundamental forms of Ananta and the others in the eight directions. (L. 4)

Having offered incense and lamps to each [deity] individually, and having presented milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and again having offered incense and lamps, and having presented betel-leaf, plantain fruit, and pieces of coconut; having duly worshipped the thirty-eight-fold ritual placement of the digits (*kalānyāsa*); and having established the water-pots for the recitation of the Vedas at the four gates beginning with the eastern gate; one should invoke the four Vedas.

Having recited the *vedapārāyaṇa* together with a Brāhmaṇa, and having recited it together with the root mantras of the temple, one should then perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*). Then, with the hand holding the *praṇava*-arghya, one should circumambulate the fire-sanctuary together with the image-makers (*mūrttipas*). To the east of the Hotṛ-priest there should be the eastern [portion], and to the south, the southern. And to the west, having worshipped the five digits (*kalā*) beginning with Peace (*śānti*), etc.

Having encircled the *kuṇḍa* with the armor mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* using the cord made of three threads, one should worship it with "Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya huṃ. Having placed [the cord] in the center of the *kuṇḍa* with three blades of *darbha* grass, one performs the *vajrīkaraṇa*. Having deposited [the door-panel] with the *Śivāstra*, one should rotate it with the armor mantra in the middle using a blade of *darbha* grass and deposit it with "Ślīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Pāśupatāstra."
Having placed a tuft of three *darbha* blades upon that [seat] and a mat of three *darbha* blades to its north,
[one should worship] Vāgīśvara, who is red in hue, three-eyed, and four-armed, endowed with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, and holding a noose, a trident, and a varada [mudrā].

"Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara. Having thus worshipped him, [one should worship] Vāgīśī to his north— she who has the luster of a lotus flower, possesses four hands, and holds a thick staff in her hand.
Having visualized her as holding a book for exposition and bearing the *kamaṇḍalu* [water-pot] marked with a *lakṣa*, one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī.
Having offered water for honor (*arghya*) to both [hands], one should bring fire produced from a forest or other source into the vessel.

Having placed [the offering] in front of the Hotṛ priest, one should cast away the portion for the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) in the southwest with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ īṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having gazed at the fire with the root-mantra of Śiva-Śivam, one should strike it with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, sprinkle it with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and [worship it] with: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ vahnimūrttaye namaḥ*.

Thus, having drawn forth the consciousness of fire by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, and having united it with the *bindu* and the fire through the fifth inhalation (*pūraka*), one should mix it with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) during the radiant retention (*kumbhaka*). Then, having unified the triad of the elemental, the lunar, and the digestive fires, one draws them outward through the *piṅgalā* channel by means of the exhalation (*recaka*) and the *udbhavamudrā*, [uttering]: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
"Salutation to the principle of the fire-consciousness (*vanhicaitanya*). Having thus cast [the substance] into the elemental fire, one should worship it with the root-mantra of the *Saṃhitā*.

Having protected it with the *abhaya* and *śivāstra* mantras, one should enclose it with the *varma* mantra. Having transformed it into nectar with the "nectar" mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should worship it with the *hṛdaya* mantra. This is the pure seed of Śiva, whose form is light.
Having ascertained that the fire is indeed manifest, one takes the vessel for the fire, circumambulates the hearth (*kuṇḍa*) three times,
and places the Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśvara*) and the Mistress of Speech (*Vāgīśvarī*) at the mouth of the hearth. Having poured the clarified butter (*ājya*) into the vessel with the *praṇava* [Oṃ],
one visualizes the triad of channels— *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*— in its right, left, and middle portions, and the *tarā* channel in the center of those two intermediate parts.
Having visualized both the white and black fortnights, having consecrated [the materials] with the *saṃhitā*, having protected them with the *kavaca* mantra,

having rendered them nectar with the root-mantra of *abhivṛddhi*, and having worshipped them with the root-mantra of *mokṣa*, one should display the *mahāmudrā* with the great root-mantra of *śuddhaśiva* and put on the lower garments.

Having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the west, south, and north with the *varma*, *netra*, and *astra* mantras; having touched the middle enclosing stick with the *hṛdaya* and *śiras* [mantras];
he places the two *āghāra* fuel-sticks (*samidh*) above, in the south and north. Having placed another *ājya*-fuel-stick near the *praṇītā* water-vessel.
Having sprinkled [water] around [the fire] with the mantra *aditenu manyasva*, and having worshipped the purifier (*pāvaka*) with the elephant-seal (*gajamudrā*) and other gestures,

one should worship Ananta, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in the east, south, west, and north respectively. Having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective places, [one proceeds] along the path for the purpose of removing saliva.

And for the purpose of nourishing the fire, one should offer five *palāśa* fuel-sticks, moistened at the roots and tips, into the fire with the five-syllable mantra: *oṃ hāṃ śivāstrāya namaḥ*. *oṃ śrīṃ (ślīṃ) paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ*. *oṃ chūṃ kṣurikāstrāya vyomaṃ vyāpine vyomāstrāya*.

Oṃ hūṃ aghorāstrāya svāhā. Having anointed the fuel-stick (*idhma*) with clarified butter (*ājya*), [one says]: "O Brahman, in this great festival-rite, I shall place the fuel-stick. [The Brahman replies]: "Place it. Thus, at the root of that [fuel-stick], one should offer the pure five-petaled *māri* [flower] with the mantra:
"To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Sadyojāta, svāhā! Having thus mentally touched the junction of the northern enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), [one proceeds].

[The offering] is continuous for the *kṣaṇā* [deity]. Having touched the junction of the southern enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with the axe, saying "To Indra, svāhā! To the heart, svāhā!", [the offering] is not continuous for the *kṣṇaya*. Then, having taken the *sruva* ladle from behind, he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions. In the dark fortnight, having taken the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the left portion and having offered it into the southern eye of the fire-altar (*agni*) saying "To Agni, svāhā!"—(l. 9).

Taking clarified butter from the left portion and offering it into the left eye of the fire with the mantra *somāya svāhā*, then taking clarified butter from the middle portion and offering it into the forehead-eye of the fire with the mantra *agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*,
and finally taking clarified butter from the third portion and [offering it] with the mantra *agnaye svāhā*.

Oṃ hāṃ heṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the faces of Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna. Next, one should perform the ritual of making [the deity] possessed of faces: Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the faces (or from the faces) of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. One should then perform the ritual of making [the deity] possessed of tongues: Oṃ hāṃ ruṃ, svāhā to Hiraṇyajihvā, who has the luster of molten gold and resides in the face of Sadyojāta.
Oṃ hāṃ lṛṃ, svāhā to the one with the radiance of silver, who resides in the eastern face and has a single golden tongue. (l.

5) Oṃ hāṃ vrūṃ, svāhā to the one of red color, who is the western face and has a red tongue. (l. 6) Oṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to the one of black color, who resides in the southern face and has a black tongue. (l. 7)
Oṃ ṣrūṃ, svāhā to Mauktikaprabhā, who resides in the face of Tatpuruṣa, the tongue of excellent radiance. (l.
8) Oṃ srṛṃ, svāhā to [the goddess] equal to a ruby, who resides in the face of Īśāna, the exceedingly red tongue. (l.
9) Oṃ hrūṃ, svāhā to [the goddess] possessing the splendor of the autumn moon, who resides in the face of Aghora, the multiformed tongue. (p. 21a, l. 1)

Oṃ rū lrūṃ, svāhā to Hiraṇyakā and Kanakajihvā. Oṃ lṛ vrūṃ, svāhā to Kanakā and Raktājihvā. Oṃ vrūṃ śrūṃ, svāhā to Raktā and Kṛṣṇājihvā. Oṃ śrīṃ ṣrīṃ, svāhā to Kṛṣṇā and Suprabhā. Oṃ ṣrūṃ srūṃ, svāhā to Suprabhā and Atiraktajihvā. Oṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Atiraktā and Bahurūpajihvā.

The joining of the tongues. Then one should perform the making of the tongue [submissive]. Oṃ hāṃ rūṃ lrūṃ vrūṃ śrūṃ ṣrūṃ srūṃ hrūṃ hiraṇyā kanakā raktā kṛṣṇā suprabhā atiraktā bahurūpā jihvābhyāṃ svāhā. Then, having performed the full oblation with the Prāsāda mantra ending in vauṣaṭ, and having placed the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) upon the fire: "I shall perform the expiation for the *caru*. Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Indra!"
Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Soma! "May you swell; may [strength] come together unto you for union" (*āpyāyasva sametu te saṃgathe*); "O Soma, may virility come from every side;

be present at the gathering of strength" (*viśvatassoma vṛṣṇiyaṃ bhavā vājasya saṅgathe*); "place within us the most abundant nourishment" (*sante payāṃsi... nidhiṣva*). Having thus poured clarified butter over these two *caru* offerings, [he says]: "O Agni, you are the lord of splendor, the supreme purifier."
Therefore, by establishing [the Lord] within the lotus of your heart, I satisfy and worship the Lord.

Having thus made this request, and having recited the Śivagāyatrī one hundred and eight times with clarified butter (*ājya*), and having offered oblations one hundred and eight times with the mantra ending in *oṃ hāṃ śivāya svāhā*, and having offered one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ sadāśivāya svāhā*— one should offer the fuel-sticks with the Sadyojāta-mantra, the clarified butter with the Vāmadeva-mantra, the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the Aghora-mantra, and the parched grain (*lāja*) with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.

With the *Īśāna* mantra, mustard seeds; with the *Hṛdaya*, barley; with the *Śiras*, sesame; at the *Śikhā*, black gram; for the [mantra of] the colors, mung beans; with the *Netra*, bamboo; with the *Astra*, jujube; and with the *Mūla*, plantain fruit. Having offered twenty-five oblations with the *mṛgīmudrā*, having offered each substance individually, and having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of each substance, one should offer the entire remainder of the substance with the *saṃpāta* using the *havyavāhana* mantra.
Let [the oblation] settle upward. Having offered the *sruva*-oblation from above, having silently placed the *īkṣaṇa* spoon into the fire, one should perform the *saṃsrāva-homa*.
(l. 9) On the first day... until the end of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), having offered morning and evening oblations every day, having offered with this mantra and these substances. (p. 23a, l.

1) At the end of the sacred ford, having united the form residing in the fire with the *śivakumbha* by means of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), and having performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*). (l. 2)
Having offered water for the feet and other honors:
"Since the fire-abiding Lord is the supreme purifier,
therefore, O Fire-god, I establish you within this vessel of yours."

Having joined the fire with the *mūla* [mantra] into the water-pot (*kumbha*), they sprinkle themselves with the *sruva* ladle. He removes the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). Having washed the *sruca* in the *vaiśvānara* fire, having poured out the remainder, and having filled it with water, he throws the enclosing-sticks outside.
With the verse, "This ocean in the highest heaven beyond a hundred," having offered the remaining *anuyāja* oblations, he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon the fire.
He offers the *jaya* oblations and so forth. (l. 6) "I shall perform this *jayādi-homa* for the sake of the successful completion of the rite of the great festival (*mahotsava-karman*).

*Oṃ cittaṃ ca svāhā*. (l. 7) "To *citta*, this [oblation]. *Cittiś ca svāhā*. "To *citti*, this [oblation]. (l. 8) *Vijñānaṃ ca svāhā*. "To *vijñāna*, this [oblation]. *Manaś ca svāhā*. "To *manas*, this [oblation]. (l. 9)
And to the Śatvarīs, Svāhā! To the Śatvarīs, this [offering]. And to the Darśa, Svāhā! To the Darśa, this [offering].
And to the Pūrṇamāsa, Svāhā! To the Pūrṇamāsa, this [offering]. Then, having offered the Anājñā and the Tatraya, [he says]:
"Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā! To Prajāpati... to Agni, the lord of the seven, this [offering]. To Vardhana... Rudrakāmā, Svāhā!"

To Agni, the treasure-receptacle—this [is mine], not mine. Of the Brahman-foundation, of the mind, of the Vedic utterance, of the oblations born of the Brahman, of the clarified butter—the redundant portion here. "This Viṣṇu... svāhā! "The three-eyed one... "O Gaṇas, you... "To Jātavedas... svāhā! "Of Viṣṇu indeed... sing... svāhā! "Thou art the sovereign of Viṣṇu... svāhā! "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu... svāhā! (l. 6)
O Agni, you are the *agnīdh*; to Viṣṇu, Svāhā! You are the breast of Viṣṇu; to Viṣṇu, Svāhā! You are the firm support of Viṣṇu;

to Viṣṇu, Svāhā! You belong to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu, you; Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, this! You are the forehead of Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu, you; Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, this! Whatever in this rite I have overdone, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni [make it right].

May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the knower of the two, the doer of all, make my sacrifice well-sacrificed and well-offered. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, who is praised with good hymns and who fulfills the desires of the oblations—*svāhā*. This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. With the *sruva* spoon, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*):
the middle one, the southern one, and the northern one; in each case, taking a small portion from the sacrificial grass strewn around (*paristaraṇa*).

In the *ājyasthālī* [clarified butter vessel], there are the top, middle, and bottom portions. Having separated one [portion] from the others, like a *prastha*, he follows with the three-fold binding according to the *bṛhatī* meter. Having cast the middle and the other two into the two eyes of the armor, and having joined them with the heart and the head, he offers the *saṃsrāva* oblation: "To the Vasus, the portions of the *saṃsrāva*, svāhā! This [is done] in the east, north, and so forth, upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the *viṣṭara*.

Having given the *bali* offering, having offered the oblation, having recited the *parama* verse, and having sipped water (*ācamya*), he should pour out the remainder [of the water] while saying, "You have approved; you have been satisfied.

Then, having drawn [portions] from the *praṇītā* waters toward the various directions, and having washed and sprinkled the remaining water on the ground, the Brahmin bestows a boon, or he should feed a Brāhmaṇa. He should perform the worship of Agni with the verse, "O Agni, by that splendor which is yours... (RV 10.87.24).

Having offered the *śivāgni*, one should then construct two square mandalas in the eastern direction, forming nine compartments (*navakoṣṭha*). In the first mandala, in the cardinal directions, [one should offer] "Salutation to Rudra, Mātṛgaṇa, and Adhikṣetra. In the intermediate directions, [one should offer] "Salutation to the Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas. Having offered the *bali* and *arghya*, and having likewise offered [the oblation] to the Kṣetrapāla in the center of that very mandala, one should prepare the festival vehicle (*utsavayāna*). At the time of the procession, the Ācārya...

He should stand on the right side of Maheśa together with the [eight] Mūrttis. In front of Maheśa are singing, dancing, rhythmic clapping, and instrumental music; in front of these is the great Śaiva; in front of him are the Rudra-attendants (*rudragaṇikā*); in front of them are the ascetics (*tapasvinaḥ*); in front of them are the kings; in front of them are the princes; in front of them is the great musical ensemble; in front of that is Skanda; in front of him is Vināyaka. On both sides are banners and flags, and behind Maheśa are the parasols. And in the [adjacent] quarter is Caṇḍeśvara.

Behind that [image], the devotees [should stand]. Thus they shall conclude the festival. Likewise, in the middle of the street and at its end, one should offer plantains (*kadalīphala*), as well as coconuts (*nālikera*), citrons (*mātuluṅga*), sugarcane pieces (*ikṣukhaṇḍa*), betel leaves (*tāmbūla*), and so forth. Having thus performed the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other honors facing the Goddess, one should present fruits and the like, as well as betel, incense, and lamps, in the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*).

Having offered the *ārātrika* service, he should perform the pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) and the pure song (*śuddhagīta*). He should cause various stories of diverse lands and various kinds of women to be heard, as well as the *dharmamayūkha* and so forth. Standing on the right side of the *ācārya*, he should look [at the deity]. Kings [should stand] on the left side; thus, having gratified Maheśa, he should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the sake of the procession (*yātrā*).

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa and the general arghya for the worship of Vināyaka, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the ceremonial bathing for the sake of the procession. Then follows the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the placement of the nine pitchers (*navakalaśa*).

Having worshipped Hṛśvara within the central pitcher (*kumbha*), and having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra of Manonmanī in the *vardhanī* vessel, one should worship Indra and the other deities in the [remaining] pitchers.

There is also the installation of nine jars for the Vīraśakti. Having worshipped the Vīraśakti in the central jar, and having worshipped the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā in the [other] jars, and having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should perform the consecration.
Then, having completed the remainder of the twilight worship, and having concluded the midday worship, one should spend the remainder of the night in stories of Śiva.

One should [perform] this by means of listening. (l. 8) Likewise, at the time of dawn, one should perform the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth, according to the sequence of the *balakrama*, as well as the ritual bathing for the purpose of the procession (*yātrā*). Thus ends the procedure for the festival on the first day. The commencement of the second day occurs only at night. (l. 10) Having completed the worship of the pavilion and so forth, ending with the fire oblation (*homa*), in the evening, the second...

To the deities of the day: [to] Brahmā, the sacrificial offering (*balidravya*) is milk-rice (*pāyasa*), turmeric powder, *tāmarai* flowers, and *pullāja*. To Uṣā, the offering is... [the flower] *puṅgaipū*. Starting from the right side of the door up to the serpent-king and ending with the bull, having offered the oblation: at the place of Bṛhaspati, "Svāhā to Brahmā"; to its left, "Svāhā to Brahmā."

Having offered the bali from the beginning with "ityādi īśānāya svāhā | brahmaṇe svāhā |" up to the end with "astrāya svāhā," one should present the offerings upon the great bali-pedestal as before, up to the conclusion of the service for the bali-image. Having adorned Skanda on the Piñcavāhana and performed the offering of sesame seeds, one should likewise adorn Maheśa, Vīraśakti, and the attendant deities as previously described.

One should perform the procession as before. At the time of dawn, one should likewise perform the offering (*bali*) and the procession in due order. Thus ends the festival on the second day. (l. 6) On the third day, the offering for the *balidevatās* is: "Svāhā to the spirits (*bhūtas*)!
The substances are sesame seeds, rice, *vāla*, *pala*, clarified butter (*ājya*), flowers—namely, jasmine (*kāruttu*), *erukazham*, and *mallikai* flowers. (l. 7)

The Nāgaliṅga flower. Having performed the rites from the worship of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) as before up to the end of the *homa*, and having offered the *bali* to [the deities] beginning with Nandin and ending with Vṛṣabha, one should offer the *bali* starting with "Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā" and "To the Bhūtas, svāhā," and so on, up to Īśāna.
Then, having performed the ritual service for the *baliberas*, at the time of the procession (*yānakāla*), one should adorn Candraśekhara for the vehicle of the Bhūtas.

Having given a gift of gold for the sake of Maheśāna, the entire [ritual] procession should be performed as before. (l. 2) At dawn as well, one should perform the worship and the sequence of offerings (*balikrama*) in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), as well as the procession. Thus ends the procedure for the festival of the third day. (l. 3) For the fourth day, the deities of the day are the Gandharvas. The offering substance (*balidravya*) is prepared with *maṇjala* flowers; (l. 4) [the offerings are] pure rice, flowers, *bilva*, *makila*, and *pū*.

Having offered the *bali* sacrifice to you and your retinue, from the entrance of the *maṇḍapa* and so forth up to the far end, one should present the *bali*: "To Brahmā in the station of Brahmā, svāhā!

To the Gandharva, svāhā! and so on, as before, up to the northeast (*īśāna*). At the time of departure, having adorned Maheśvara upon his bull-vehicle and having performed the offering of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should proceed as before. One should also do likewise at the time of dawn.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the festival of the fourth day and subsequent days. For the deity of the fifth day, Indra, the sacrificial substance (*balidravya*) is *indravallī* mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), and the flower is the blooming *campaka*. From the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) up to the end of the fire-oblation (*homa*), and from the gates up to the gate-towers (*gopura*), the offerings are as before. In the station of Brahmā, [one offers] to Brahmā, *svāhā*.
Having offered the *balikriyā* (oblation rite), [one offers] to the deities of the daily oblations (*dinabali*) of the seventh day: "Homage to Śrīpati. The oblation materials are:

rice mixed with molasses (*gulānna*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the fruit of the *bṛhatī*, flowers, and *veṇtāmara* flowers. Having performed the oblation starting from the *puṣpaka* and *nandī* up to the gateway (*gopura*), one offers the oblation to Brahmā at the Brahma-sthala with: "To Brahmā, svāhā! To Śrīpati, svāhā! and so forth, offering the oblation as far as the northeast (*īśāna*).

Having performed the ritual service (*upacāra*) at the great altar of offerings (*mahābalipīṭha*) as before, he should then enter the temple. Thereafter, at an auspicious moment, he should apply black ointment (*kṛṣṇagandha*). The preceptor, having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkṛtya*), [takes] a garment and an upper cloth. Having washed the vessel (*sthālikā*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and concealed it with the armor-mantra (*varman*), he places the fragrant black ointment into the vessel.

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* with the limbs of Brahmā, having offered the nine substances beginning with black incense (*kṛṣṇagandha*), and having performed the circumambulation of the temple, one should place [the vessel] three feet high in front of Naṭeśa. Having performed the ritual of the parts (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and worshipped Vināyaka, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) twice, saying: "I shall offer black incense to Naṭaśa. Then, having caused the proclamation of merit (*puṇyāha-vācana*), having performed the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and having established the *śāntikumbha* jar.

Having offered the seven substances and established the *śāntikumbha* (peace-pitcher), one should combine the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), barley (*yava*), and sesame seeds (*tila*) with perfumes such as black sandalwood (*kṛṣṇagandha*). Having sprinkled these with water from the *śāntikumbha*, and having performed the rites of protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*), one should present the gift to Śiva, dedicating it to the preceptor (*ācārya*). First, the gift of an elephant (*gajadāna*) is given.

Having given gifts of gold, gifts of vessels containing gold, gifts of sesame seeds, and gifts of clarified butter; having observed the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*); and having worshipped Naṭarāja through the rites of invocation and so forth—(the procedure for worship is as follows: "So 'ham, obeisance to Ānanda-Tāṇḍaveśvara; so 'ham, obeisance to the embodiment of Ānanda-Tāṇḍava. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Śiva, Ānanda-Tāṇḍaveśvara. ... [etc.]
Having worshipped with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ paratattvaparātparānandatāṇḍaveśvarāya namaḥ*, and having offered incense and lamps, one should take black sandalwood paste and apply it to the right arm;
then, saying *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, one applies it to the head.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the head—on the forehead. Oṃ huṃ, homage to the crest-lock—on the throat. Oṃ haiṃ, homage to the armor—on the heart. (l. 7)
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the Eye—on the foot of stability.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Weapon. Taking the substances previously consecrated, one should place them in the locations previously mentioned. Having offered coconuts and other items with the Īśāna mantras, (line 9).

Having performed the incense, lamps, and nightly offerings (*ārātrika*), as well as the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and having caused black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*) to be applied to all the images, one should thereafter give sacred ash, betel, and black fragrant paste to the devotees. Thus ends the procedure for the application of black fragrant paste.

Having approached the presence of Maheśa and placed the great [image] upon the pedestal (*kheṭaka*), [the priest], having entered the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), [proceeds].

Having worshipped Vināyaka, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) twice, saying: "I shall perform the ritual of mounting the chariot. Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having set out the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should sprinkle the chariot with pure water, then with the *puṇyāha* and *pañcagavya* substances, and again with pure water. Having thus performed the ritual bathing of the chariot, one should worship the chariot. On the two wheels: *oṃ hāṃ divānāthāya candrāya namaḥ*. On the staff: *oṃ hāṃ haraye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vajriṇe namaḥ*.

[He should worship] with "Obeisance to the sixty Ajāleśa Rudras. [He should worship] with "Obeisance to Dharma and the others" on the limbs; with "Obeisance to those in the intervals between the limbs" on the other parts of the body. (l. 5) In the west—obeisance to Viṣṇu; in the north—obeisance to Brahmā. Thus he should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas). (l. 6) Having given these final gifts and having waited for a moment, standing in the middle of the chariot, he should worship the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) in the swinging mechanism (ḍolāyantra). (l. 7) Having established Maheśvara upon the lion-throne, [he should worship him] with all ornaments, sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth.

Having adorned [the deity], having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other services, (l. 8) having presented fruits and other offerings, and having given incense and lamps, one should cause the great procession of Maheśvara to take place.

Standing to the south of the preceptor (*ācārya*), having established the sacrifice with six or seven attendants according to the rule, and having lit the great lamp... [one should say]: "Obeisance to the Vedas on the cord; obeisance to the serpents in the four directions. Having thus worshipped, having given incense and lamps, having presented [the offering] to Vāyu... and having given betel-leaf, one should offer incense and lamps.
Having reached the presence of Maheśa and having offered a silver gift as before, one should perform a gift for the propitiation of the planets according to one's desire.
Having meditated upon Śiva, one should recite [the mantra]. Then, for the sake of pleasing the faceless Gaṇas stationed at the front of the chariot, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*)...
Having performed the offering, the devotees should pull the chariot. One should cause the chariot to proceed both before the Lord and [before] the Gāyatrī... [and so forth].

[The attendants] should remain at the swing-mechanism (*ḍolāyantra*). At the wheel-mechanism (*cakrayantra*) and the balance-mechanism (*tulāyantra*), having placed Maheśadevī behind the Lord (*īśvara*), one should perform the chariot-procession as before. One should perform [the rite] for Maheśa. Having caused the making of the chariot, thereafter, on the [western] side, having adorned Caṇḍeśvara in the chariot, one should perform the drawing of the chariot. The seven deities [should be placed] in their own places.
Having placed all the deities in their respective positions within the palanquin and having seated the Goddess [therein as well], he should enter the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*).

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other services, having presented fruits and other offerings, and having offered incense and lamps, he should perform the ritual of *nīrājana* and conduct the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the sake of the procession (*yātrā*). Then, he should perform the remainder of the twilight rites (*sandhyā*).

The festival of the eighth day is concluded. On the night of the ninth day, at the conclusion of the *homa*, having tied the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon Maheśa, Vīraśakti, and the deities in the form of weapons (*astramūrti*), one should perform the consecration of the sacred water (*tīrthādhivāsana*). Having prepared a second sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the purpose of the *tīrthādhivāsana*, and having had the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) made, and having encircled it with a cord, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel within a nine-square grid.

Having adorned [the vessel] with water, coconut leaves, and so forth, one should worship the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*). In the central *vardhanī*, one should worship the seat, the form, and the root-mantra of Manonmanī.
[The rivers] Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī...
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in these waters.
Having worshipped these [deities] by their own names in the eight vardhanīs starting from the east,

having offered [the oblation], and having presented incense and lamps, one should worship the Vajra and other [emblems] around them. One should perform the protection, the veiling, and the consecration with nectar, and cover them with cloths.

On the day of the ninth [tithi]... salutations to Śiva. The sacrificial materials (*balidravya*) are pure rice, parched grain (*lāja*), *vela*, red flowers, *tumbī* flowers, and *kaumya* cakes (*apūpa*).
Having taken recourse to the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*), [one offers]: "Svāhā to Brahmā! Svāhā to Śiva! and so forth, up to the end of the ritual services (*upacāra*).

As before, having adorned the queen in a palanquin, having given the gift of salt for the journey, having caused the vehicle to be prepared, having offered food offerings, incense, and lamps, and having performed the sixteen services, [the rite] is completed. Having performed the circumambulation of the bridegroom,
and having caused the sounding of conchs, musical instruments, song, lute, flute, drum, and the *bhramaṇa* dance, thus one performs the circumambulation.

Having entered the *ālaya* and placed the *akarpūra*, one should perform the rites up to the ritual bathing (*snapanānta*) as before. One should offer the remainder at the twilight worship (*sandhyā*).

On the following day, having performed the worship of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) and so forth, ending with the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*) and the procession (*yāna*), as before; and having entered the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*) and established Śiva, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*). Having smeared a square area with cow dung either in front of the deity or on the bank of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), [one should proceed].

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center and in the eight directions, and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus there, one should place a mortar in the center, wrap it with a cloth, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, worship Vināyaka, and make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*); I shall perform the powder festival. Then, on the southern site, [one should perform] the *puṇyāha* ceremony.
Having had [the text] recited, and having established a trident in the western direction, one should worship the root-mantra of the Astra-āsana-mūrti with "Oṃ Hāṃ.
Having offered fruits and other items, and having given betel, incense, and a lamp, one should offer salutations: "Salutation to Jayaśakti in the south-eastern region;
salutation to Vighneśvara in the south-west; salutation to Svāhāśakti in the north-west; salutation to Gaṅgā in the north-east."

In the eastern part, having wrapped it with cloth and having placed the drum (bherī), one should worship the drum. In the center: *namaḥ rudrāya*. In the south: *namaḥ brahmaṇe*. In the north: *namaḥ viṣṇave*. In the southern ring: *namaḥ sūryāya*. In the northern ring:
*namaḥ candrāya*. On the seven petals: *namaḥ saptamātṛbhyaḥ*. On the nine pegs: *namaḥ navagrahebhyaḥ*. On the staff: *namaḥ skandāya*.

Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamps, there is no need to strike the drum. Having placed the *mūla* [mantra] upon a cloth, and having also placed the trident (*śūla*) [there], [one recites]:
*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Upon the mortar (*ulūkhala*): *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Upon the pestle (*musala*): *rudrāya namaḥ*. Taking turmeric (*haridrā*), [one places it] upon the mortar:
*oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
